newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan economy seen in choppy seas in first half.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan economy seen in choppy seas in first half.

text.p: Pakistan's economy faces a tough time in the next six months but interest rates could fall and monetary policy could be eased if it weathers the storm, a research report from a Karachi brokerage said.
"We project choppy waters ahead for the economy in the first half of 1997," said the report, made available on Monday, by Khadim Ali Shah Bukhari and Company.

It said the government's main challenge was to meet its end-June target of slashing the budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product from 6.3 percent in fiscal 1995/96 (July-June) as demanded by the International Monetary Fund.
"If met, it will lay the ground for lowering interest rates and relaxing monetary policy," the report said. "That would let private sector investment return in the second half."

The present caretaker government led by Meraj Khalid hopes that its stabilisation and reform measures will pave the way for a return to a three-year lending programme from the IMF's enhanced structural adjustment facility.
But the government is due to relinquish power after a general election set for February 3 and there is no guarantee that its elected successor will pursue the same policies.
The report said that uncertainty over the outcome of the polls and a looming June budget would delay investment decisions and contain growth in non-agricultural sectors.
It forecast economic growth of 5.0-5.5 percent in 1996/97 and an inflation rate of 11 to 12 percent.
The immediate concern was the balance of payments, after a crisis at the end of 1996 was averted only by accumulating more foreign debt, shorter maturities and non-concessional terms.
The report predicted a payments hump in March and June, adding that an expected improvement in the trade account would not be significant enough to stem foreign exchange outflows.

The government was expected to turn to the privatisation of state assets to improve the quality of capital flows from debt towards equity and to build reserves of $1.6 billion, or seven weeks of import cover, from $834 million now, the report said.
Hidden liabilities of about $4.5 billion in non-resident accounts underlined the low level of reserves and was the Achilles' heel of Pakistan's external accounts.
"If foreign exchange reserves fall below $450 million the IMF may once again freeze the stand-by programme," the report said. "March is a crunch month again."
The IMF agreed to resume and expand a stalled standby loan after President Farooq Leghari sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on November 5 for alleged corruption and misrule.
The report said the rupee was likely to lose more ground against the dollar, partly due to the strength of the U.S. currency, after shedding 15.4 percent of its dollar value in 1996.

The report said a large savings-investment gap lay behind Pakistan's twin problem of budget and current account deficits. "To mobilise savings requires an environment of low inflation and positive real rates of return," it argued.

"We expect to see in 1997 privatisations of public sector banks, positive measures to clean up portfolios, an increase in deposit rates, and measures to slow the mobilisation of foreign currency accounts," the report said.
